title: The Trojan Plain
note: The geographic register: real lat/lon, only features with a defensible position. The poem's own spatial logic — the camp order, the wagon-road and its waypoints, the ford, the tomb of Ilus — belongs to the schematic plate and is deliberately absent here. RECONSTRUCTION FOLLOWED: Kraft, Kayan and Erol 1980, as refined by Kayan (2003, 2019) and by Kraft, Rapp, Kayan and Luce 2003 — the Late Bronze Age embayment lies north and north-west of Hisarlik, so the dry, usable plain, and therefore the battlefield, lies SOUTH AND WEST of the city. That is the reverse of nearly every popular illustration, which puts the fighting on the ground north of Troy. Others differ: Luce (1984) puts the shoreline west by south of the site with a broad embayment between the city and the Sigeum ridge, and the Achaean camp on the lower slopes of that ridge some four miles west of Hisarlik — which rotates the battlefield from north-south to roughly east-west. Both cannot be drawn on one sheet; this one draws Kraft. The BASE of this sheet is survey: the modern coast is contoured from the Copernicus DEM's 30 m water mask, and the rivers are OpenStreetMap's mapped channels, so the reconstruction has something measured to be read against. The Bronze Age reconstruction drawn over that base is NOT TRACED from any published figure -- see the shore layer's note for how its line was derived from stated measurements. Feature names on the sheet come from the gazetteer; Sigeion and Rhoiteion are Strabonic, not Homeric, and appear here as later reference points.

sources.cite: Kraft, John C., Ilhan Kayan, and Oguz Erol. "Geomorphic Reconstructions in the Environs of Ancient Troy." Science 209, no. 4458 (1980): 776-82.

layers.note: The MODERN sea: the Aegean off the Sigeion shore and the mouth of the Dardanelles, as they stand now. Contoured from the ocean class of the Copernicus DEM GLO-30 Water Body Mask at 30 m posting and filled, so that the Bronze Age water drawn over it -- the embayment, the lagoon, the swamp -- is read against a real sea rather than against blank parchment. This is not the sea of 1200 BC: at that date the water reached far further south, over ground the Scamander has since filled in. Drawn first, under every other layer, because it is the sheet's water and not a feature on it.

sources.cite: Copernicus DEM GLO-30, Water Body Mask. (c) DLR e.V. 2010-2014 and (c) Airbus Defence and Space GmbH 2014-2018, provided under COPERNICUS by the European Union and ESA.

layers.note: The landward shore of the embayment at about 1200 BC. Drawn as a soft band, not a hard line: it is approximate to on the order of a kilometre. NO PUBLISHED FIGURE WAS TRACED. The line is derived arithmetically from three stated measurements: (1) at maximum Holocene transgression the embayment reached c.10 km south of Hisarlik (Kraft, Kayan and Erol 1980); (2) progradation had carried the coastline west of Troia by c.4000 BP (Kayan); (3) the modern coast lies c.6 km from the site. Those give a delta front advancing c.5 km per millennium through the narrow ria between 6000 and 4000 BP, then c.1.5 km per millennium across the wide bay from 4000 BP to the present. Carried forward 800 years from Kayan's 4000 BP checkpoint, 1200 BC puts the front roughly 1 to 1.5 km north-north-west of Hisarlik, which is where this line runs; its flanks are then closed against the surveyed feet of the Sigeion and Rhoiteion ridges. Kayan's separate figure of c.17 km is the ria measured inland from the PRESENT coast at 7000-6000 BP and is not the same quantity as Kraft's 10 km; the two are not conflated here. Rendered as stipple pending a waterline style in the renderer; the stipple is the honest register for a reconstructed band and should stay stippled even once waterlines exist, which belong on surveyed coasts.

sources.cite: Kraft, John C., Ilhan Kayan, and Oguz Erol. "Geomorphic Reconstructions in the Environs of Ancient Troy." Science 209, no. 4458 (1980): 776-82.

Kayan, Ilhan. "Geoarchaeological Interpretations of the 'Troian Bay.'" In Troia and the Troad: Scientific Approaches, edited by Gunther A. Wagner, Ernst Pernicka, and Hans-Peter Uerpmann. Berlin: Springer, 2003.
Kraft, John C., George Rapp, Ilhan Kayan, and John V. Luce. "Harbor Areas at Ancient Troy: Sedimentology and Geomorphology Complement Homer's Iliad." Geology 31, no. 2 (2003): 163-66.

layers.note: The wide sandy barrier that a relative sea-level fall of 2 to 2.5 m left across the mouth of the bay in the Late Bronze Age, closing the remaining water body into a shallow lagoon. Position approximate to on the order of a kilometre, on the same derivation as the shore band: it is set between the reconstructed delta front and the modern coast, closed at both ends against the Sigeion and Rhoiteion ridges. Not traced from any figure.

sources.cite: Kayan, Ilhan. "Landscape Development and Changing Environment of Troia (North-western Anatolia)." In Landscapes and Landforms of Turkey, edited by Catherine Kuzucuoglu, Attila Ciner, and Nizamettin Kazanci, 277-91. Cham: Springer, 2019.

layers.note: The shallow lagoon of about 1200 BC: the water left between the prograding delta front and the sandy barrier after the Late Bronze Age sea-level fall. Its outline is the shore band and the barrier joined, so it carries their uncertainty, on the order of a kilometre. Troy overlooks a wetland, a lagoon and a distant sea, not a deep-water bay.

sources.cite: Kayan, Ilhan. "Geoarchaeological Interpretations of the 'Troian Bay.'" In Troia and the Troad: Scientific Approaches, edited by Gunther A. Wagner, Ernst Pernicka, and Hans-Peter Uerpmann. Berlin: Springer, 2003.

layers.note: Swamp lay over much of the delta plain through the Late Bronze Age (Kayan). Drawn as a belt along the Scamander behind the head of the bay, where the river's own floodplain is lowest; extent generalized, not surveyed. Intended texture is stipple at a finer radius than the relief hachure, so marsh reads lighter than ridge; the renderer currently fills a region as a flat tint.

sources.cite: Kayan, Ilhan. "Landscape Development and Changing Environment of Troia (North-western Anatolia)." In Landscapes and Landforms of Turkey, edited by Catherine Kuzucuoglu, Attila Ciner, and Nizamettin Kazanci, 277-91. Cham: Springer, 2019.

layers.note: The dry, usable plain of about 1200 BC, and the point of the whole sheet: it lies south and west of Troy, hemmed by the Sigeion ridge on the west and the ridge Hisarlik stands on to the north-east, because the ground north of the city was lagoon, barrier and swamp. Kraft, Kayan and Erol drew exactly this conclusion — if the war happened, the battlefield lay to the south and west of the city. The Achaeans poured out 'onto the Scamandrian plain' and stood in 'the flowery Scamandrian meadow' (Il. 2.465-467); the poem names the plain but fixes no boundary, so this outline is a generalization of the modern lowland minus the reconstructed water, not a surveyed limit.

sources.cite: Kraft, John C., Ilhan Kayan, and Oguz Erol. "Geomorphic Reconstructions in the Environs of Ancient Troy." Science 209, no. 4458 (1980): 776-82.

layers.note: The modern coast, and the only surveyed waterline on this sheet: the Aegean shore south to Besik Bay, the mouth of the Karamenderes, Kum Kale, and the Dardanelles shore running east past the Rhoiteion spur. Every vertex is a measurement -- the ocean class of the Copernicus DEM GLO-30 Water Body Mask, 30 m posting, contoured at the land/water boundary and generalised to about half a pixel at this plate's size. It is drawn ON by default because the reconstruction above it has to be read against something surveyed: the ground between this line and the Bronze Age shore is delta the Scamander has laid down since. This layer carried fifteen hand-typed vertices before 2026-07-28.

sources.cite: Copernicus DEM GLO-30, Water Body Mask. (c) DLR e.V. 2010-2014 and (c) Airbus Defence and Space GmbH 2014-2018, provided under COPERNICUS by the European Union and ESA.

layers.note: Scamander, called Xanthus by the gods (Il. 20.74); the modern Karamenderes. The line is the MODERN channel, from OpenStreetMap, chained out of the ways OSM splits a river into and generalised to the sheet: the meanders are surveyed, not drawn. Its Bronze Age bed is not this line and is not drawn -- the channel then lay west of today's, in water that is now land, and no publication gives a coordinate for it. Read this as the river's valley, which has not moved, rather than as its 1200 BC course, which has.

sources.cite: OpenStreetMap contributors, waterway data, ODbL 1.0.
Pleiades: Scamander.

layers.note: The Simoeis, coming down from the north-east along the far side of the ridge Hisarlik stands on; 'between the streams of Simoeis and Xanthus' is where the fighting runs (Il. 6.4). The equation with the modern Dumrek Su is a Strabonic tradition that Leaf, Cook and Luce all accept, not an excavated fact, and the gazetteer holds the river at that tier. The line is the modern Dumrek from OpenStreetMap, carried west as far as the channel is mapped: it stops about a kilometre short of the Karamenderes, which is where the survey stops, not where the river does. Homer's confluence of the two (5.774) is deliberately not marked -- both channels have shifted and the whole delta has prograded, so its Bronze Age position cannot be fixed.

sources.cite: OpenStreetMap contributors, waterway data, ODbL 1.0.
Strabo, Geography 13.1.
Cook, J. M. The Troad: An Archaeological and Topographical Study. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1973.

layers.note: The Sigeion ridge: the low ridge, 30 to 40 m, closing the plain on the west, running from Kum Kale south past Yenikoy, with the Kesik cut through it. A surveyed landform, so solid hachure rather than form lines; its outline here is a generalization of the ridge's extent, not a contour. Sigeion is not named in the Iliad — it is Strabonic geography, and the traditional western headland of the Achaean beach. Luce would put the Achaean camp on this ridge's lower western slopes.

sources.cite: Cook, J. M. The Troad: An Archaeological and Topographical Study. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1973.
Pleiades: Sigeion.

layers.note: The Rhoiteion ridge on the Cakal Tepe spur, closing the plain on the north-east and fronting the Dardanelles. A surveyed landform; outline generalized. Rhoiteion is not named in the Iliad either; it is the traditional eastern headland of the Achaean beach, paired with Sigeion, and the tomb of Ajax was shown on its spur at In Tepe.

sources.cite: Cook, J. M. The Troad: An Archaeological and Topographical Study. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1973.
Pleiades: Rhoiteion.

layers.note: The ridge Troy stands on: Hisarlik is its western tip, a low spur running east with the Simoeis valley on its north side. This is why the city commands the plain to its west and south. A surveyed landform; outline generalized.

sources.cite: Dorpfeld, Wilhelm. Troja und Ilion: Ergebnisse der Ausgrabungen in den vorhistorischen und historischen Schichten von Ilion, 1870-1894. 2 vols. Athens: Beck & Barth, 1902.
